subject: Musculoskeletal
vignette: A 20-year-old college football player receives a lateral blow to his left knee while his foot is planted on the turf. He hears a pop, develops acute pain and swelling, and notes that the knee gives way when he tries to cut. Examination shows a positive anterior drawer sign and medial joint-line tenderness.
question: Which combination of structures is classically injured in this pattern (the "unhappy triad")?
explanation_correct: The unhappy triad occurs in contact sports when a lateral force strikes the knee while the foot is planted, producing a valgus stress. It classically consists of injury to the anterior cruciate ligament, medial collateral ligament, and medial meniscus, the last because it is attached to the MCL. Patients present with acute pain and signs of knee instability.

explanation_incorrect.A: The LCL and lateral meniscus are injured by varus rather than valgus force and are not part of the classic unhappy triad.
explanation_incorrect.C: The PCL resists posterior tibial translation and is typically injured by a posterior blow or dashboard injury, not a lateral valgus force.
explanation_incorrect.D: An LCL injury would follow varus stress; the valgus mechanism here damages the MCL rather than the LCL.
explanation_incorrect.E: Both PCL and LCL injuries are inconsistent with the valgus, foot-planted mechanism of the unhappy triad.

educationalObjective: The unhappy triad from a valgus force with planted foot injures the ACL, MCL, and medial meniscus.
source: Generated from 11. Musculoskeletal.pdf - Pathology: Common knee conditions

subject: Musculoskeletal
vignette: A 46-year-old woman who spends long hours kneeling while gardening develops localized swelling and tenderness directly over the front of her right kneecap. There is no joint effusion, and range of motion of the knee is full and painless. She recalls repeated pressure on the area.
question: Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation_correct: Prepatellar bursitis is inflammation of the prepatellar bursa in front of the kneecap and can be caused by repeated trauma or pressure from excessive kneeling, hence the name housemaid's knee. Localized prepatellar swelling and tenderness with a non-effused, painlessly mobile joint is typical. This distinguishes it from intra-articular pathology.

explanation_incorrect.A: A popliteal (Baker) cyst arises in the gastrocnemius-semimembranosus bursa and produces posterior knee swelling, not anterior prepatellar tenderness.
explanation_incorrect.B: Patellar tendinopathy causes pain at the inferior patellar pole that worsens with jumping, not a superficial prepatellar collection from kneeling.
explanation_incorrect.D: Septic arthritis produces a hot, swollen joint with effusion, fever, and severely painful restricted motion, which are absent here.
explanation_incorrect.E: Infrapatellar fat pad impingement causes pain just below the patella with extension and is not a superficial prepatellar swelling from pressure.

educationalObjective: Prepatellar bursitis (housemaid's knee) is anterior knee swelling from repeated kneeling, with a non-effused joint.

subject: Musculoskeletal
vignette: A 67-year-old woman with long-standing osteoarthritis notices a soft swelling in the popliteal fossa that enlarges with activity. Ultrasound shows a fluid collection that communicates with the knee joint. Her clinician diagnoses a Baker cyst.
question: From which bursa does this popliteal cyst typically arise?
explanation_correct: A popliteal cyst, also called a Baker cyst, is a popliteal fluid collection in the gastrocnemius-semimembranosus bursa. It commonly communicates with the synovial space and is related to chronic joint disease such as osteoarthritis or rheumatoid arthritis. The communication explains why joint effusion can distend the cyst.

explanation_incorrect.A: The prepatellar bursa lies anterior to the patella and is the site of housemaid's knee, not a posterior popliteal cyst.
explanation_incorrect.B: The suprapatellar bursa is an extension of the knee joint above the patella and is not the origin of a popliteal fossa cyst.
explanation_incorrect.C: The pes anserine bursa is anteromedial below the joint line and produces medial knee pain, not posterior fossa swelling.
explanation_incorrect.E: The iliopsoas bursa is at the hip and may be involved in hip disease or psoas pathology, not in a popliteal cyst.

educationalObjective: A Baker cyst is fluid in the gastrocnemius-semimembranosus bursa that communicates with the knee joint in chronic arthritis.

subject: Musculoskeletal
vignette: A 22-year-old soccer player sustains combined ACL and MCL injuries from a valgus force with the foot planted. The teaching attending points out that although the unhappy triad is classically taught as including the medial meniscus, clinical series show a different meniscus is more frequently torn in this combined injury pattern.
question: Which meniscus is more commonly involved with combined ACL and MCL injury?

options.text: Medial meniscus, because it is firmly attached to the MCL
Neither meniscus is typically involved in this injury pattern
Both menisci are involved with equal frequency
Medial meniscus, because it is less mobile than the lateral meniscus

explanation_correct: Although the unhappy triad is traditionally described as ACL, MCL, and medial meniscus injury, lateral meniscus involvement is actually more common than medial meniscus involvement in conjunction with ACL and MCL injury. The medial meniscus is classically included because of its attachment to the MCL, which explains the teaching point but not the observed frequency.

explanation_incorrect.A: The medial meniscus is attached to the MCL and is part of the classic triad, but it is not the meniscus most commonly involved with combined ACL and MCL tears.
explanation_incorrect.B: Meniscal injury frequently accompanies combined ACL and MCL injury, so neither being involved is incorrect.
explanation_incorrect.C: The two menisci are not torn with equal frequency; lateral meniscus tears predominate in this setting.
explanation_incorrect.D: Reduced medial meniscus mobility is a reasonable teaching rationale for the classic triad, but it does not reflect actual injury frequency.

educationalObjective: Despite the classic unhappy triad, the lateral meniscus is more commonly injured than the medial meniscus alongside ACL and MCL tears.

subject: Musculoskeletal
vignette: A 19-year-old basketball player is struck on the lateral aspect of his knee by another player's shoulder while his foot is fixed to the floor. He immediately feels the knee buckle inward and cannot continue playing. The team physician suspects an unhappy triad and reviews the mechanism with him.
question: Which force and limb position best produce this injury pattern?

options.text: Valgus force with the foot planted on the ground
Varus force with the foot planted on the ground
Direct posterior blow to the proximal tibia
Isolated internal rotation of the tibia with the foot lifted

explanation_correct: The unhappy triad results from a lateral force striking the knee when the foot is planted, creating a valgus moment that stresses the ACL, MCL, and medial meniscus. The lateral blow with a fixed foot in this patient is the classic contact-sport mechanism. Varus force, hyperextension, and posterior blows produce different ligamentous injury patterns.

explanation_incorrect.B: A varus force from a medial blow stresses the LCL and lateral structures rather than producing the MCL-predominant unhappy triad.
explanation_incorrect.C: Isolated hyperextension tends to injure the ACL and posterolateral structures without the characteristic combined MCL and meniscal pattern.
explanation_incorrect.D: A direct posterior blow to the proximal tibia causes a PCL injury, as in a dashboard injury, not the triad described.
explanation_incorrect.E: Rotation with the foot lifted lacks the valgus force with a planted foot required for the classic unhappy triad mechanism.

educationalObjective: A lateral (valgus) force with the foot planted is the classic mechanism of the unhappy triad.
